THIS yearâs Nobel Prize in Literature should be announced in early October, and over on the tony British betting site Ladbrokes, Haruki Murakami of Japan, riding the waves of acclaim for his fantastical novel â1Q84,â is the favorite. Other well-known names â Milan Kundera, Philip Roth, Joyce Carol Oates â arebandied about, but Mr. Murakami is unique: among perennial Nobel front-runners, it would be difficult to find a writer more influenced by the popular music and culture born of the social and cultural upheavals of the 1960s.
Using excerpts from Bob Dylanâs lyrics, Bill Wyman explains why the musician deserves literary praise.
That fact prompts a pressing question: why isnât the most vital of the artistic catalysts of those upheavals himself a front-runner for the prize? Iâm referring of course toBob Dylan, a fierce and uncompromising poet whose writing, 50 years on, still crackles with relevance. Mr. Dylanâs work remains utterly lacking in conventionality, moral sleight of hand, pop pabulum or sops to his audience. His lyricism is exquisite; his concerns and subjects are demonstrably timeless; and few poets of any era have seen their work bear more influence.
Iâm not the first to suggest it, but itâs time to take the idea seriously. The Nobel Prize in Literature is not awarded posthumously, and Mr. Dylan, now in his 70s, has battled heart disease. Alfred Nobelâs will decreed that the prize should go to a writer with âthe most outstanding work in an ideal direction.â Why hasnât Bob Dylan received one?
Given his medium (songwriting) and profession (rock star), Mr. Dylan may have some strikes against him:
Bob Dylan is not in the mold of the sober creator of âgreat literature.âHe most certainly is not â but consider: in 1997, the literature prize went toDario Fo, the incorrigible and profane Italian playwright, at whose selection the Roman Catholic Church in particular was amusingly aghast. The vast majority of literature prize recipients are world titans (Mario Vargas Llosa, GÃ¼nter Grass) or less-well-known but established candidates (Orhan Pamuk of Turkey, the late Seamus Heaney of Ireland), with a relatively obscure recipient every so often (likeElfriede Jelinekof Austria nine years ago), just to keep us all on our toes. It has been too long since the Swedish Academy has honored a mind like Mr. Foâs.
Mr. Dylan just writes pop lyrics.Actually, Mr. Dylan writes, full stop. Why discount what has been written because of where it ends up? Those who would use the word âpopâ as a cudgel or tool of exclusion do so at their peril. Dickens and Twain, Hugo and Shakespeare and Euripides â all soaked up the acclaim of their day. Alfred Hitchcock, whose work at its height met critical condescension, would have some useful thoughts on the subject as well.
Still â his doggerel verses are not literature.In the 1950s in America, rock was a mongrel music, created out of the cultures of the downtrodden â people who built their lives around the blues, folk, gospel or country. Electric guitars got involved, and then some leers and hip thrusts. A new postwar generation of youth took notice, and a cultural revolution was born.
Mr. Dylan added literature. He was first, of course, a singer of folky loquacity, and a serious student of the musicâs antediluvian influences: what the critic Greil Marcus calls âthe old, weird America.â To this he wedded the yawp of the Beats and the austere intellectualism of the Symbolists. Drugs didnât hurt, and passing but pungent imagery shows that Mr. Dylan had absorbed the Bible as well.
That disruptive mÃ©lange gave us the imagery and power of songs like âChimes of Freedomâ and âDesolation Row,â of âA Hard Rainâs a-Gonna Fallâ and âVisions of Johanna,â among scores of others. He has displayed a mastery of everything from the political jeremiad (âItâs Alright, Ma [Iâm Only Bleeding])â to the romantic epic (âTangled Up in Blueâ), and lines like âMoney doesnât talk, it swearsâ show his way with the lancing aperÃ§u. Mr. Dylan is neither a saint nor a moralist. Epic anger and personal petulance erupt out of his lyrics. But so do tender mercies, extravagant and deep love, self-castigation and what turns out to have been no little wisdom.
Pop lyrics are corrupted by the writerâs desire for popular acclaim.In fact, the record is clear that â whatever ambition lay in his breast â his is a personality, and his art is of a nature, that makes it difficult to chase popular approval or sanction. Mr. Dylan is no Solzhenitsyn, but he is a figure who genuinely challenges the established order.
He was surely the first pop artist to tell his audience things it didnât want to hear. In 1963, from the dais at a civil rights dinner, he looked with some contempt at the well-dressed crowd and said, âMy friends donât wear suits.â The drama surrounding his lurch into electric music is perhaps overstated; âLike a Rolling Stoneâ was a huge hit. Whatâs really radical about the song is its derisive look at his privileged listeners. Mr. Dylan reveled in the comeuppance he saw on the horizon: âYou said youâd never compromiseâ and now â... you stare into the vacuum of his eyes / And ask him do you want to make a deal?â

Joel A. Miele Sr., who was the commissioner of environmental protection in New York City when it undertook major initiatives to safeguard its water supply in the 1990s, died on Monday at his home in Howard Beach, Queens. He was 78.
Joel A. Miele Sr., shown in 1994, was an engineer by training.
Follow us onTwitterand like us onFacebookfor news and conversation.
The cause was cancer, said his son, Joel Jr.
Mr. Miele, a public engineer and member of theCity Planning Commission, had been buildings commissioner under MayorRudolph W. Giulianiwhen the mayor appointed him to head the environmental agency in 1996.
At the time, the city had embarked on a five-year, $660 million pollution control project that was both ambitious and diplomatically delicate: buying land and improving environmental protection in a 2,000-square-mile region of upstate New York, where it had no jurisdiction, but beneath which lay the city’s water supply, increasingly threatened by leaking septic systems and other polluting byproducts of an upstate development boom.
From 1996 until 2002, when Mr. Miele was replaced by Christopher O. Ward, the agency negotiated the purchase of thousands of acres and undertook pollution control measures under the so-called Watershed Protection Program, the terms of which had been hammered out between upstate authorities and Mr. Miele’s predecessor, Marilyn G. Gelber.
Environmentalists criticized Mr. Miele’s efforts as too slow and too friendly to business. While he headed the agency, upstate business leaders and government officials successfully lobbied for a major state highway project, which paved over a large swath of the watershed; builders routinely disregarded pollution control guidelines set by the city; and the agency’s own employees spilled mercury-laced chemicals in a building adjoining one of the city’s upstate reservoirs, for which the city was fined $50,000 after pleading guilty to two felony counts of violating the federal Clean Water Act.
Mr. Miele said he was doing his best, arguing that contending with the many stakeholders in the region — state, federal and local governments, environmentalists and business interests — was complicating his work.
“If I had my own way as the manager of the water supply, sure, it’d be great to put a Berlin Wall around the whole thing, get everybody out and let it all go back to nature,” he told The New York Times in 1999.
“Then I could guarantee to the mayor and the City of New York we’ll never have a problem with our water. But that’s not realistic.”
In a related project, Mr. Miele oversaw the opening, in 1998, of the first segment of a new water tunnel system linking the city to its upstate water supply — a 13.5-mile tunnel under Brooklyn and Queens.
As the commissioner of buildings from 1994 to 1996, Mr. Miele carried out Mr. Giuliani’s mandate to shrink government, reducing the number of building inspectors by 20 percent and introducing a controversial “self-certifying” system, which allowed architects and engineers to approve their own blueprints and conduct their own inspections of completed jobs.
Mr. Miele said licensed engineers and architects were better qualified than inspectors to certify that their work met code regulations, and argued that streamlining the process would benefit the city economy.
City inspectors would follow up with spot checks, he said, but “nobody is going to go out and look for reasons to aggravate people when there isn’t a reason.”
Joel Arthur Miele was born on May 28, 1934, in Jersey City to Gennaro and Eleanor Miele. His father, a civil engineer, founded the firm Miele Associates, which he moved to Middle Village, Queens, in the 1940s while moving the family to Howard Beach.
After serving in the Navy, Mr. Miele received his engineering degree from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn, which is now part of New York University, and joined his father’s firm in the early 1960s.
He was named to the Planning Commission in 1990 by the Queens borough president, Claire Shulman.
Besides his son, Mr. Miele is survived by his wife, Josephine; two daughters, Vita Marie Miele-Chu and Janet Miele-Powers; seven grandchildren; a brother, Jean; and two sisters, Lana Miele and Eleanor Miele-Herceg.
